text: Evaluating a language model sounds simple: ask it questions and count the right answers. In practice almost every part of that sentence hides a decision, and small decisions can move a score by more than the difference between two models. This lesson takes the main measurements apart.

The most basic measurement comes straight from training. Perplexity is the exponential of the average negative log-probability that the model assigns to each true token in held-out text. A perplexity of twenty means the model is, on average, as uncertain as if it were choosing evenly among twenty tokens, like someone guessing the roll of a twenty-sided die. It is cheap and smooth, but it only compares models that share a tokenizer, because a model that splits text into more pieces is being scored on a different task.

Multiple-choice benchmarks are often scored without letting the model write anything. The evaluator computes the log-probability of each option as a continuation of the question, and picks the most likely one. That hides quiet choices. A longer option collects more negative log-probability simply because it has more tokens, so many evaluations normalise by length, as the GPT-3 paper did for most of its tasks. Scoring the same benchmark by likelihood, or by asking the model to write a letter, can give noticeably different numbers.

For code, the natural test is whether the program works. The Codex paper, from Chen and colleagues at OpenAI, introduced pass at k: the chance that at least one of k sampled programs passes the unit tests. Drawing exactly k samples gives a noisy estimate, so they drew more samples, counted how many passed, and used an unbiased formula: one, minus the number of ways to choose k failing samples, divided by the number of ways to choose any k.

Every score is an estimate from a finite sample of questions, so it carries uncertainty. If a model answers a fraction p correctly on n questions, the standard error is roughly the square root of p times one minus p, divided by n. On five hundred questions at seventy percent accuracy, that is about two percentage points, so a one point gap between two models may be noise. Comparing models on the very same questions helps, because the paired differences are less noisy.

A deeper problem is contamination. Benchmarks are published on the web, and web text is what models are trained on, so a model may have seen the test questions, or even the answers, during pretraining. A high score then measures memory rather than skill, like a student who saw the exam paper in advance. Careful reports check for overlap between training data and test sets, and newer benchmarks keep their test questions private or keep adding fresh ones.

For open-ended answers, many evaluations now use a strong model as the judge. Zheng and colleagues, who introduced MT-Bench, found that GPT-4 as a judge agreed with human preferences about as often as humans agreed with each other, but they also documented biases: a tendency to favour the answer shown first, to favour longer answers, and to favour answers written by the judge itself. Swapping the order of the two answers and averaging the verdicts is a simple defence.

The lesson for your own evaluations holds at every scale: write down exactly how a score is computed, measure its uncertainty, and keep the test data out of anything the model could have seen. That closes the module on large language models. Next we turn to other kinds of generative models, beginning with autoencoders and variational autoencoders.
